summary: Follow-up plan for layer L0 (Banach spaces of locally analytic functions) of the locally analytic distributions roadmap, continuing the accepted whole-roadmap packet, whose eighteen L0 nodes it cites. It plans, at target level, the nonarchimedean functional analysis that the predecessor left as an external interface, and the chart construction on compact manifolds. Locally convex spaces over a nonarchimedean field by lattices and ultrametric seminorms (strictly smaller than Mathlib's PolynormableSpace), inductive and projective limits, bounded sets and strong duals compared with Mathlib's bounded-convergence topology, spherically complete fields and the nonarchimedean Hahn–Banach theorem (moved down from a higher tier); strict morphisms, the quasi-abelian categories of all and of Hausdorff locally convex spaces, the strict derived category with its left t-structure and left heart, and the identification of extensions of classical objects with strict short exact sequences; projective and inductive tensor products with their comparison for Fréchet and LB-spaces and the c₀ tensor identities; orthonormal bases of Banach spaces, controlled lifts and complemented subspaces; compactoid sets and compact maps compared with Mathlib's IsCompactOperator, spaces of compact type, nuclear spaces, the compact-type/nuclear Fréchet anti-equivalence and compact-type tensor products; the three-space inputs of Colmez–Nizioł Appendix A, with a lattice proof that nuclearity passes to strict extensions (replacing an archimedean citation, E101), the splitting of finite-rank extensions, and a duality step for compact-type extensions whose strictness input is recorded as the packet's one gap (E102); power series on polydiscs with the substitution bound, analytic atlases compared with Mathlib's analytic manifolds, chart indices and their Banach stages, locally analytic functions on a manifold as a compact-type inductive limit independent of the atlas, pullbacks and multiplications, products and distributions on compact manifolds. Sources: Schneider's Nonarchimedean Functional Analysis and p-Adic Lie Groups, Schneider–Teitelbaum, Schneiders, Emerton, Colmez, Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł, Colmez–Gilles–Nizioł, Colmez–Nizioł and Dierolf–Roelcke. The independent review adds barrelledness, pseudo-polarity, LB/Fréchet factorisation, operator/tensor comparison and Banach tensor injectivity; corrects quotient finite maxima, degenerate norm criteria and cofinality; and treats current scalar Tate algebras and Mathlib manifold carriers as existing work.

nodes.title: Nonarchimedean locally convex spaces
nodes.statement: A locally convex K-vector space (in the nonarchimedean sense) is a K-vector space V with a topology for which the translates v + L of the members L of some family 𝓛 of lattices form a basis, where 𝓛 is stable under nonzero scalar multiples (for L ∈ 𝓛 and a ∈ K^× some member lies in aL) and under finite intersections (up to containment). Equivalently the topology is the one defined by a family of seminorms q : V → ℝ_{≥0} with q(av) = |a|q(v) and the strict triangle inequality q(v + w) ≤ max(q(v), q(w)): the gauge p_L(v) = inf{|a| : v ∈ aL} of a lattice L is such a seminorm, a lattice is open exactly when its gauge is continuous, and the sets {v : q_{1}(v), …, q_{r}(v) ≤ ε} are open lattices defining the seminorm topology. Addition and scalar multiplication are continuous. NACvx K denotes the category of these spaces with continuous K-linear maps and HANACvx K its full subcategory of Hausdorff spaces; V is Hausdorff exactly when the open lattices intersect in {0}, equivalently when the continuous seminorms separate points. Subspaces carry the restricted seminorms and quotients V/U the quotient seminorms q̄_F(v + U) = inf_{u∈U} max_{i∈F} q_i(v + u), with F ranging over finite subsets of a defining family (q_i); one must close that family under finite maxima before taking quotient seminorms; V/U is Hausdorff exactly when U is closed. The separation sep V = V/closure{0} is left adjoint to the inclusion HANACvx K → NACvx K. Kernels in both categories are the algebraic kernels with the subspace topology; the cokernel of f : V → W is W/f(V) with the quotient topology in NACvx K and W/closure(f(V)) in HANACvx K. Over an ultrametric normed field these spaces are exactly the topological vector spaces whose topology is given by seminorms satisfying the strict triangle inequality; Mathlib's PolynormableSpace, which admits seminorms satisfying only the ordinary triangle inequality, is strictly larger, and Mathlib's ordered-field LocallyConvexSpace does not apply.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: From lattices to seminorms: for a lattice L the gauge p_L is a seminorm with {p_L < 1} ⊆ L ⊆ {p_L ≤ 1} (Schneider, Lemma 2.2), so the gauges of a defining family of lattices define the same topology (Proposition 4.4).

From seminorms to lattices: finite intersections {q_{i_1}, …, q_{i_r} ≤ ε} are lattices (Lemma 4.2), stable under scaling and intersection, and they define the seminorm topology (Proposition 4.3); continuity of the vector operations is Lemma 4.1, and Lemma 4.5 gives the criterion for openness of a lattice and continuity of a seminorm.

Hausdorff criterion and separation: the closure of {0} is the intersection of the open lattices (Lemma 4.6); a continuous linear map into a Hausdorff space vanishes on it, which gives the universal property of sep V.
Subspace and quotient topologies are again locally convex, defined by restricted and quotient seminorms (Schneider §5.B); the quotient is Hausdorff iff the subspace is closed.
Cokernels: a continuous g : W → Z with g∘f = 0 factors uniquely and continuously through W/f(V); when Z is Hausdorff g vanishes on closure(f(V)), so the Hausdorff cokernel is W/closure(f(V)).

Comparison with Mathlib: an ultrametric seminorm is in particular a Mathlib Seminorm, so these spaces are PolynormableSpace; the converse fails by the ℓ¹ test below, because an open O_K-submodule of a seminorm topology must be absorbed by the seminorm balls.
For quotients use the finite maxima q_F before infimizing, as Schneider §5.B explicitly requires. Infimizing individual coordinate seminorms need not give the quotient topology.
acceptance: The four unit tests below.
On every example in the tests the lattice description and the seminorm description give the same open sets.

nodes.title: Locally convex inductive and projective limits
nodes.statement: Let (V_h, f_{hk}) be a diagram in NACvx K. (i) The locally convex inductive limit lim→ V_h is the algebraic colimit V with the finest locally convex topology making all structure maps j_h : V_h → V continuous: a lattice of V is open iff its preimage in every V_h is open; a linear map out of V is continuous iff all composites with the j_h are; a seminorm on V is continuous iff all its pullbacks are; when V = Σ_h j_h(V_h) and the V_h carry defining lattice families, the sums Σ_h j_h(L_h) form a defining family; the locally convex direct sum ⊕_h V_h is the case of the discrete diagram. (ii) The projective limit lim← V_h is the subspace of compatible families in ∏_h V_h with the initial topology, defined by the seminorms q∘pr_h; it is the limit in NACvx K and is Hausdorff (and closed in the product) when all V_h are. (iii) For an increasing sequence V_1 ⊆ V_2 ⊆ … with T_{n+1}|V_n = T_n (a strict inductive limit), the limit topology induces T_n on V_n, the limit is Hausdorff if every V_n is, each V_n is closed if closed in V_{n+1}, and in that case a subset is bounded iff it lies and is bounded in one V_m. An inductive limit of Hausdorff spaces need not be Hausdorff; for injective compact transition maps it is (compact-type-spaces). A separated colimit is obtained by applying sep.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Final topology: the lattices whose preimages are all open form a defining family; continuity of maps and seminorms out of V is Schneider Lemma 5.1(i)–(ii) and the basis by sums of lattices is Lemma 5.1(iii).
Direct sums: Lemma 5.2 compares ⊕ and ∏; Lemma 5.3 gives subspaces, quotients and closedness of sums, and Corollary 5.4 the Hausdorff property.

Strict inductive limits: Proposition 5.5 extends open lattices step by step (L_{n+m} = V_{n+m} ∩ L_{n+m+1}) to get the induced topology, Hausdorffness and closedness; Proposition 5.6 is the bounded-set criterion, proved by contradiction with a sequence escaping every V_n.
Projective limits: the initial topology is defined by the pulled-back seminorms, and compatible families form a closed subspace of the product when the V_h are Hausdorff.
acceptance: The three unit tests below.

nodes.title: Bounded sets and the strong dual
nodes.statement: For V in NACvx K a subset B ⊆ V is bounded if every open lattice L absorbs it: B ⊆ aL for some a ∈ K. For V, W in NACvx K let L(V, W) be the continuous linear maps and, for a family 𝔅 of bounded subsets covering V, give L(V, W) the 𝔅-topology defined by the lattices L(B, M) = {f : f(B) ⊆ M}, B ∈ 𝔅, M an open lattice of W. With 𝔅 the finite subsets this is the weak topology L_s(V, W); with all bounded subsets it is the strong topology L_b(V, W). V′_s = L_s(V, K) and V′_b = L_b(V, K) are the weak and strong duals; both are Hausdorff. A linear map f is continuous iff for every continuous seminorm p on W some continuous seminorm q on V has p∘f ≤ q; for normed V and W the strong topology is the operator-norm topology; the transpose f′ : W′_b → V′_b of a continuous f is continuous; V is bornological if every lattice absorbing all bounded sets is open, metrizable spaces are bornological, and for bornological V and complete Hausdorff W the space L_b(V, W) is complete. Over a nontrivially normed ultrametric field K, bounded subsets are exactly Mathlib's von Neumann bounded subsets (Bornology.IsVonNBounded K), and the strong topology on L(V, W) is Mathlib's default topology on V →L[K] W, which is the topology of uniform convergence on von Neumann bounded sets; V′_b is Mathlib's StrongDual K V with that topology.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Boundedness and the 𝔅-topologies: Schneider §6 defines bounded sets and the 𝔅-topologies; Proposition 6.1 is the seminorm criterion for equicontinuity, hence continuity.
Normed case: Remark 6.7 identifies the strong topology on L(V, W) with the operator norm when V, W are normed.
Bornological spaces: Propositions 6.13–6.14 characterise bornological spaces and show metrizable spaces are bornological; Proposition 7.16 gives completeness of L_b(V, W).
Transpose: Remark 16.1(ii) computes the preimage of L(B, o) under f′ as L(f(B), o).

Mathlib comparison: an open lattice is a zero neighbourhood and every zero neighbourhood contains an open lattice, so 'absorbed by every open lattice' coincides with 'absorbed by every zero neighbourhood'; Mathlib's ContinuousLinearMap.topologicalSpace is UniformConvergenceCLM over the von Neumann bounded sets, the same basic lattices L(B, M).
acceptance: The four unit tests below.
For V = c₀(ℕ, K) the operator norm on V′ is the sup norm of the coefficient sequence (Colmez, Proposition I.1.6).

nodes.title: Spherically complete fields
nodes.statement: K is spherically complete if every decreasing sequence of closed balls B_{r_1}(c_1) ⊇ B_{r_2}(c_2) ⊇ … (r_n > 0) in K has nonempty intersection; equivalently every family of pairwise intersecting closed balls has nonempty intersection. Spherically complete fields are complete. A field whose value group |K^×| is discrete (then |K^×| = r^ℤ for some 0 < r < 1) is spherically complete; finite extensions of ℚ_p are discretely valued and locally compact, hence spherically complete. ℂ_p is not spherically complete: a dense sequence (a_n) can be avoided by a nested sequence of balls with radii decreasing to a positive limit.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Pairwise criterion: order the radii of a pairwise intersecting family and use that of two intersecting balls the one of smaller radius is contained in the other (Schneider Lemma 1.3, from Lemma 1.1).

Replace each positive real radius by the largest value-group radius defining the same ball. For a discrete value group these effective radii either stabilize, so the nested balls coincide eventually, or tend to zero, so the centres form a Cauchy sequence and completeness gives a point in every ball (Schneider Lemmas 1.4 and 1.6). Real radii themselves need not belong to the value group.

ℂ_p: enumerate a dense sequence (a_n) and choose nested balls B_n of diameters decreasing to a positive limit with a_n ∉ B_n; a point in the intersection would have a ball around it avoiding the dense sequence (Schneider §1, printed pp. 7–8).
acceptance: The four unit tests below.

nodes.title: The nonarchimedean Hahn–Banach theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete, U a K-vector space, q a nonarchimedean seminorm on U and U_0 ⊆ U a subspace. Every linear form ℓ_0 : U_0 → K with |ℓ_0(v)| ≤ q(v) on U_0 extends to a linear form ℓ on U with |ℓ(v)| ≤ q(v) for all v. Consequences: (a) if V is a Hausdorff nonarchimedean locally convex space and v_0 ≠ 0, some continuous linear form takes the value 1 at v_0; (b) every continuous linear form on a subspace V_0 ⊆ V (subspace topology) extends to a continuous linear form on V; (c) every finite-dimensional subspace of a Hausdorff V is topologically complemented; (d) for an ultrametric normed space V, a continuous linear form on a subspace extends with the same operator norm (take q = ‖ℓ_0‖·‖·‖). Without spherical completeness the theorem fails: there are nonzero locally convex spaces with no nonzero continuous linear form. Mathlib's Hahn–Banach theorems (Mathlib.Analysis.Normed.Module.HahnBanach, Mathlib.Analysis.LocallyConvex.HahnBanach) assume IsRCLikeNormedField and do not apply to ℚ_p; this theorem is therefore planned here.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete (finite extensions of ℚ_p qualify).
proofSteps: One step: for v_1 ∉ U_0 the balls B(v) = {a : |a − ℓ_0(v)| ≤ q(v − v_1)}, v ∈ U_0, intersect pairwise by the strict triangle inequality, so by spherical completeness (pairwise form) some b lies in all of them; setting ℓ(v_1) = b keeps |ℓ| ≤ q on U_0 + Kv_1 (Schneider, Proposition 9.2). If q(v_0 − v_1) = 0 for some v_0 the intersection is the single point ℓ_0(v_0).
Zorn's lemma over pairs (U_1, ℓ_1) extending ℓ_0 with |ℓ_1| ≤ q finishes the proof.

(a) choose a continuous seminorm with q(v_0) = 1 and extend av_0 ↦ a (Corollary 9.3); (b) dominate ℓ_0 by the restriction of a continuous seminorm of V (Corollary 9.4); (c) extend coordinate projections of a finite-dimensional subspace (Corollary 9.5).
Continuity of the extension follows from the seminorm bound (Proposition 6.1).
acceptance: For K = ℚ_p, U = ℚ_p² with the max norm, U_0 = ℚ_p × 0 and ℓ_0(x, 0) = x, every ℓ(x, y) = x + cy with |c| ≤ 1 is an extension: the extension is not unique.

Applied to the closed proper subspace c₀(ℕ, K) of ℓ^∞(ℕ, K), (a) for ℓ^∞/c₀ gives a nonzero continuous linear form on ℓ^∞ vanishing on c₀, the key step of Schneider Proposition 11.1 (c₀ is not reflexive).
With K = ℂ_p (not spherically complete) the statement is not asserted.

nodes.title: Strict morphisms and the quasi-abelian categories NACvx and HANACvx
nodes.statement: A morphism f : V → W of NACvx K is strict if the induced bijection V/ker f → f(V) is a homeomorphism for the quotient and subspace topologies, equivalently f is relatively open: for every open lattice L of V some open lattice M of W has M ∩ f(V) ⊆ f(L). This is Mathlib's Topology.IsStrictMap for linear maps (the factorisation onto the range is a quotient map; for linear maps this is equivalent to V/ker f → range f being a homeomorphism). In HANACvx K, where the image is closure(f(V)), f is strict iff it is strict in NACvx K and f(V) is closed. Both NACvx K and HANACvx K are quasi-abelian: they are additive with kernels and cokernels, a pullback of a strict epimorphism is a strict epimorphism and a pushout of a strict monomorphism is a strict monomorphism. Strict monomorphisms are the topological embeddings (closed embeddings in HANACvx K) and strict epimorphisms the open surjections (surjections onto Hausdorff quotients in HANACvx K). A sequence V′ → V → V″ is strictly exact if the first map is strict and its image is the kernel of the second; a sequence of Hausdorff spaces is strictly exact in HANACvx K iff it is strictly exact in NACvx K. The short strictly exact sequences make both categories exact categories in Quillen's sense, the notion that the Tau Ceti roadmap GrothendieckEulerForms plans as ExactStructure in its Layer 0 (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GrothendieckEulerForms#layer-0-intrinsic-exact-structures-and-conflation-exact-functors); that notion is cited, not planned here.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Relative openness: for linear maps the quotient-to-image comparison is open iff the images of open lattices contain traces of open lattices on f(V) (Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł §2.1.1); Mathlib's LinearMap.isStrictMap_iff_isHomeomorph_quotKerEquivRange gives the comparison with Topology.IsStrictMap.

Pullbacks: the pullback of g : W → Z along a strict epimorphism f : V → Z is the subspace {(v, w) : f(v) = g(w)} of V × W; its projection to W is open onto W because f is open and surjective, by intersecting product lattices.

Pushouts: for a strict monomorphism f : E → F and g : E → G the pushout is (F ⊕ G)/{(f(e), −g(e))}; given an open lattice L_G of G choose, using that E has the topology induced from F, an open lattice L_F of F with f^{-1}(L_F) ⊆ g^{-1}(L_G); then the image of L_F ⊕ L_G meets G in L_G, so G → pushout is a topological embedding. In the Hausdorff category the graph is closed and the embedding is closed.

Hausdorff strict exactness: kernels agree in both categories and for Hausdorff spaces a strict morphism of NACvx K with closed image is strict in HANACvx K, which gives the comparison of strictly exact sequences (Colmez–Gilles–Nizioł §2.1.2).

nodes.statement: Let E be NACvx K or HANACvx K (quasi-abelian). In the homotopy category K(E) of cochain complexes, the strictly exact complexes form a saturated null system, and the derived category is the Verdier quotient D(E) = K(E)/N(E); a strict quasi-isomorphism is a morphism with strictly exact mapping cone. D(E) carries the left t-structure: D^{≤0} consists of the complexes strictly exact in positive degrees, D^{≥0} of those strictly exact in negative degrees; the truncations send E to (… → E^{n−1} → ker d^n → 0) and to (0 → coim d^{n−1} → E^n → …), so the cohomology object LH^n(E) is the monomorphism coim d^{n−1} → ker d^n placed in degrees −1, 0, and LH^n(E) = 0 iff E is strictly exact in degree n. The heart LH(E) is abelian; each object is represented by a monomorphism E_1 → E_0 (E_0 in degree 0), two representations being identified through squares that are both cartesian and cocartesian. The functor I : E → LH(E), V ↦ [0 → V], is fully faithful; a sequence V′ → V → V″ of E is strictly exact iff I(V′) → I(V) → I(V″) is exact in LH(E). The classical part C : LH(E) → E sends [E_1 → E_0] to coker(E_1 → E_0); C is left adjoint to I and C∘I ≅ id, so E is reflective in LH(E). An object [E_1 → E_0] lies in the essential image of I (is classical) iff E_1 → E_0 is strict; classical objects are stable under subobjects and extensions; and I induces an equivalence D(E) ≃ D(LH(E)). In NACvx K a non-Hausdorff cokernel stays classical, while in HANACvx K the classical part is the Hausdorff cokernel.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Null system: a triangle with two strictly exact vertices in a degree has its third vertex strictly exact there, by a cartesian-square argument (Schneiders Proposition 1.2.14, Corollary 1.2.15); define D(E) as the quotient (Definition 1.2.16).

t-structure: Lemma 1.2.17 transfers the t-structure of K(E) to the quotient; Definition 1.2.18 names it; Proposition 1.2.19 computes the truncations and LH^n; Corollary 1.2.20 characterises vanishing and the aisles by strict exactness.
Heart: Corollary 1.2.21 describes LH(E) as a localisation of the category of monomorphisms; Definitions 1.2.22–1.2.26 define representations, I and C.
Adjunction and exactness: Proposition 1.2.27 (C ⊣ I, C∘I ≅ id), Corollary 1.2.28 (I fully faithful, reflects and preserves strict exactness).
Classical objects: Proposition 1.2.29 (strict representations, stability under subobjects and extensions); Proposition 1.2.32 (D(E) ≃ D(LH(E))).

Carriers: use Mathlib's HomotopyCategory of cochain complexes indexed by ℤ, which is pretriangulated for additive categories, its localisation at the strict quasi-isomorphisms (Functor.IsLocalization), and Mathlib's TStructure, which requires a pretriangulated category; the strict-exactness predicate comes from strict-morphisms-quasi-abelian.

nodes.title: Extensions of classical objects are strict short exact sequences
nodes.statement: Let 0 → A′ → A → A″ → 0 be an exact sequence in LH(NACvx K) with A′ = I(V_1) and A″ = I(V_2) classical. Then A is classical, A ≅ I(V) with V = C(A), and 0 → V_1 → V → V_2 → 0 is strictly exact in NACvx K: V_1 → V is a topological embedding onto the kernel and V → V_2 an open surjection. If V_1 and V_2 are Hausdorff then V_1 is closed in V, V is Hausdorff and the sequence is strictly exact in HANACvx K. Conversely every strict short exact sequence of NACvx K gives an exact sequence in LH(NACvx K). Hence an exact sequence of LH(C_K) with classical outer terms, as in Colmez–Nizioł Appendix A, is the same as a strict short exact sequence of locally convex spaces, and statements about it are statements about strict extensions.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Classicality of A: classical objects are closed under extensions (Schneiders Proposition 1.2.29(c)).
Strict exactness: apply Corollary 1.2.28 to 0 → I(V_1) → I(V) → I(V_2) → 0, which is exact, so 0 → V_1 → V → V_2 → 0 is strictly exact; the converse is the other direction of Corollary 1.2.28.

Hausdorff case: V_1 is the kernel of a continuous map to the Hausdorff space V_2, hence closed; a vector of V outside V_1 is separated from 0 through V_2, and a nonzero vector of V_1 by the subspace topology, so V is Hausdorff; strict exactness in HANACvx K follows from strict-morphisms-quasi-abelian.

nodes.title: The projective tensor product and its completion
nodes.statement: For V, W in NACvx K, V ⊗_{K,π} W is the algebraic tensor product with the locally convex topology defined by the lattices L ⊗_{O_K} M (images of L ⊗ M) for open lattices L ⊆ V, M ⊆ W; equivalently by the tensor seminorms (p ⊗ q)(u) = inf{max_i p(v_i)q(w_i) : u = Σ v_i ⊗ w_i}, and p_L ⊗ p_M = p_{L⊗M}. It represents jointly continuous bilinear maps: a bilinear β : V × W → U is jointly continuous iff the linear map V ⊗_π W → U is continuous. (p ⊗ q)(v ⊗ w) = p(v)q(w), and p ⊗ q is a norm when p and q are; the converse holds when both underlying vector spaces are nonzero; V ⊗_π W is Hausdorff when V and W are, and for subspaces V_0 ⊆ V, W_0 ⊆ W the projective topology on V_0 ⊗ W_0 is the subspace topology. The completed projective tensor product V ⊗̂_{K,π} W is the Hausdorff completion; it represents jointly continuous bilinear maps into complete Hausdorff spaces, and the algebraic tensor product is dense in it. For Banach spaces it is the Banach space completion of V ⊗ W for the tensor norm.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Universal property: Schneider Lemma 17.1 characterises joint continuity by lattices, which is the definition of the projective topology.

Gauges: Lemma 17.2 computes p_L ⊗ p_M = p_{L⊗M}; Lemma 17.3 and Proposition 17.4 give the pure-tensor formula and the norm criterion; Corollary 17.5 gives Hausdorffness and the subspace property. The finite-dimensional almost-orthogonal basis estimate used in Lemma 17.3 is the finite-dimensional part of banach-c0-models. The norm converse excludes zero tensor factors (source issue E104).

Completion: the Hausdorff completion of Schneider Proposition 7.5 (Mathlib's UniformSpace.Completion on the uniform structure of the topological group) composes the universal property with completeness of the target.
Banach case: Colmez §I.1.4 defines the tensor valuation as the best value over all expressions, which is the norm p ⊗ q.
acceptance: The three unit tests below.

nodes.title: The inductive tensor product and its comparison with the projective one
nodes.statement: For V, W in NACvx K, V ⊗_{K,ι} W is V ⊗ W with the finest locally convex topology for which the canonical bilinear map is separately continuous; it represents separately continuous bilinear maps, and V ⊗̂_{K,ι} W is its Hausdorff completion, representing them into complete Hausdorff targets. The identity V ⊗_ι W → V ⊗_π W is continuous. (a) For Fréchet spaces V and W the two topologies coincide. (b) Inductive tensor products commute with locally convex inductive limits: for V = lim→ V_i and W = lim→ W_j the natural map lim→_{(i,j)} V_i ⊗_ι W_j → V ⊗_ι W is a topological isomorphism. (c) For semi-complete LB-spaces V and W (countable inductive limits of Banach spaces, sequentially complete), in particular for spaces of compact type, V ⊗_ι W = V ⊗_π W; so for spaces of compact type ⊗̂ denotes either completion. In general the two differ.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
For (c): K spherically complete, as in Emerton (0.1).
proofSteps: Universal property and the comparison map: separate continuity is weaker than joint continuity, so the inductive topology is finer (Schneider §17.A).

(a) A separately continuous bilinear map on a product of Fréchet spaces is jointly continuous, by a Banach–Steinhaus argument on the family of maps v ↦ β(v, w_n) for a null sequence (w_n) (Schneider Proposition 17.6).
(b) Compatible separately continuous maps out of the V_i ⊗ W_j assemble, and the universal property of the inductive tensor topology identifies the two topologies (Emerton Lemma 1.1.30).

For a Banach target E, curry a separately continuous β as W → L_b(V,E). For each bounded B ⊆ W, pointwise boundedness of β(·,B) and barrelledness of V make this a bounded family in L_b(V,E). Since W is bornological the curried map is continuous. The operator space is Fréchet by lb-frechet-factorisation; that node factors the curried map through a Banach space, giving an open neighbourhood of W with bounded image. Bounded families on barrelled V are equicontinuous, which gives joint continuity. For an arbitrary locally convex target apply this argument to each Hausdorff Banach seminorm quotient. This supplies the argument underlying Emerton Proposition 1.1.31, without treating its citation to Bourbaki as an unplanned interface.

nodes.title: Completed tensor products of c₀ spaces
nodes.statement: For a set I and a K-Banach space B (K ⊆ ℂ_p closed, or any complete nonarchimedean K), c₀(I, K) ⊗̂_π B is isometrically isomorphic to c₀(I, B), sending e_i ⊗ b to the family with b at i and 0 elsewhere. Consequently c₀(I, K) ⊗̂_π c₀(J, K) ≅ c₀(I × J, K) isometrically (e_i ⊗ e_j ↦ e_{(i,j)}); if (e_i) and (f_j) are orthonormal bases of B_1 and B_2 then (e_i ⊗ f_j) is an orthonormal basis of B_1 ⊗̂ B_2; for closed subfields L ⊆ K′ of ℂ_p an orthonormal basis of an L-Banach space B stays orthonormal in K′ ⊗̂_L B; and for a complete ultrametric Banach K-algebra A with isometric scalar action, c₀(I, K) ⊗̂_π A ≅ c₀(I, A). These isomorphisms are natural in B. In particular LA_h(ℤ_p, L) = L ⊗̂_{ℚ_p} LA_h(ℤ_p, ℚ_p) for every closed L ⊆ ℂ_p, and the stages of several-variable analytic functions on products of charts are the completed tensor products of the factor stages.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: The algebraic tensor product c₀(I, K) ⊗ B is the space of families in c₀(I, B) spanning a finite-dimensional subspace of B, which contains the finitely supported families and is dense (Colmez, proof of Proposition I.1.8).

The tensor norm equals the sup norm on it: one inequality is the triangle inequality for each expression; for the other, choose a basis of the finite-dimensional span and split off the finitely many large coordinates (Colmez, proof of Proposition I.1.8).
Completeness of c₀(I, B) and density give the isometric isomorphism; the corollaries on bases and scalar extension follow (Colmez, Corollary I.1.9).
The c₀(I × J) form is the case B = c₀(J, K); the algebra case uses the same proof with coefficients in A.

nodes.title: Orthonormal bases of Banach spaces
nodes.statement: (a) If K is discretely valued, every K-Banach space V is topologically isomorphic to c₀(X, K) for some set X, and isometrically so when ‖V‖ ⊆ |K|; any norm can be replaced by an equivalent one with values in |K| (round up to the next value), and c₀(X) ≅ c₀(Y) forces |X| = |Y|. (b) For any K, a K-Banach space containing a dense subspace of countably infinite dimension (a Banach space of countable type) is topologically isomorphic to c₀(ℕ, K); more precisely, for every 0 < r < 1 it has a basis (v_n) with ‖Σ a_n v_n‖ ≥ r·max_n ‖a_n v_n‖ and, after scaling, ε ≤ ‖v_n‖ ≤ 1 for some ε > 0. In Mathlib's terms c₀(X, K) is ZeroAtInftyContinuousMap X K for discrete X with the sup norm. For L discretely valued, a family (e_i) in the unit ball is an orthonormal basis of an L-Banach space B with ‖B‖ = |L| iff its reductions form a basis of the residue-field vector space B_0/π_L B_0.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Universal property of c₀(X): a bounded map X → V into a Hausdorff quasi-complete space extends uniquely to a continuous linear map c₀(X) → V (Schneider §10, printed pp. 66–67).

(a) Normalise ‖V‖ ⊆ |K|; lift a basis of the residue vector space B_1(0)/B^-_1(0) to the unit ball; the induced map from c₀(X) is an isometry (a residue computation for finite sums) with dense image, by successive approximation using that 0 is the only accumulation point of |K| (Proposition 10.1, Remark 10.2); Lemma 10.3 compares cardinalities.

(b) Choose an increasing flag V_n of finite-dimensional subspaces with dense union and, given 0 < r = r_1 < r_2 < … < 1, inductively pick v_n ∈ V_n with ‖v_n + w‖ ≥ (r_n/r_{n+1})‖v_n‖ for w ∈ V_{n−1}; this yields the r-orthogonality estimate and an isomorphism c₀(ℕ) → V (Proposition 10.4).
Residue criterion: Colmez Proposition I.1.5 lifts a residue basis digit by digit and checks the isometry.

nodes.title: Open mapping and controlled lifts for Banach spaces
nodes.statement: Let f : V → W be a continuous K-linear surjection. (a) If V is Fréchet and W Hausdorff and barrelled (for instance Fréchet or Banach), f is open; a quotient of a Fréchet (Banach) space by a closed subspace is Fréchet (Banach) with the quotient seminorms (norm). (b) If V and W are K-Banach spaces there is C > 0 such that every w ∈ W has a preimage v with ‖v‖ ≤ C‖w‖ (controlled lift). (c) Consequently, if W ≅ c₀(X, K) with unit vectors e_x, there are v_x ∈ V with f(v_x) = e_x and sup_x ‖v_x‖ ≤ C, and s(Σ a_x e_x) = Σ a_x v_x is a continuous linear section of f. Over a nontrivially normed field, (a) for Banach spaces and (b) are Mathlib's ContinuousLinearMap.isOpenMap and ContinuousLinearMap.exists_preimage_norm_le, which make no archimedean assumption.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: (a) Schneider Proposition 8.3 (quotients) and Proposition 8.6 (open mapping, via the closed graph theorem, Proposition 8.5); for Banach spaces it is Mathlib's ContinuousLinearMap.isOpenMap.

(b) openness gives a ball of radius δ in the image of the unit ball; scaling by elements of K^× of absolute value comparable to ‖w‖ gives C = |π|^{-1}δ^{-1}, or directly Mathlib's ContinuousLinearMap.exists_preimage_norm_le.
(c) the family (v_x) is bounded, so the universal property of c₀(X) gives s; f∘s is the identity on unit vectors and hence on c₀(X) by continuity (Schneider, proof of Proposition 10.5).
acceptance: For f : K² → K, (x, y) ↦ x + y, with the max norm, C = 1 works (lift w to (w, 0)).
For the dense injection T(x)_n = p^n x_n of c₀(ℕ, ℚ_p), which is not surjective, no C exists on its image: the surjectivity hypothesis is needed.

nodes.title: Complemented subspaces and split Banach extensions
nodes.statement: Let V be a K-Banach space and U ⊆ V a closed subspace. If (a) K is discretely valued, or (b) V/U is of countable type (for instance V of countable type), then U is complemented: there is a continuous projector P of V onto U, i.e. Mathlib's Submodule.ClosedComplemented U holds. Consequently a strict short exact sequence 0 → V_1 → V → V_2 → 0 of K-Banach spaces splits topologically under (a), or under (b) when V_2 is of countable type. In this roadmap K is a finite extension of ℚ_p, so (a) always applies. Colmez–Nizioł, Remark A.2 state the splitting when K is spherically complete or V_1, V_2 are separable; the spherically complete alternative is used here only through (a) (see source issue E103).
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: V/U is Banach (banach-open-mapping-lifts (a)); by banach-c0-models it is isomorphic to c₀(X) in case (a) and to c₀(ℕ) in case (b).

Lift the unit vectors with bounded norms and build the section s (banach-open-mapping-lifts (c)); then P = id − s∘g∘pr is a continuous projector onto U, where g : V/U ≅ c₀(X) (Schneider Proposition 10.5).
A split strict sequence is isomorphic to V_1 ⊕ V_2, which is the conclusion of the splitting statement.

If the quotient has finite dimension, including dimension zero, lift a finite basis and obtain a continuous section directly; the c₀(ℕ) argument is reserved for infinite-dimensional quotients of countable type.
acceptance: Over ℚ_p (discretely valued) c₀(ℕ, ℚ_p) is complemented in ℓ^∞(ℕ, ℚ_p), unlike the real case, where c₀ is not complemented in ℓ^∞ (Phillips).

The non-Banach exact sequence 0 → LC(ℤ_p) → LA(ℤ_p) → LA(ℤ_p) → 0 of spaces of compact type, with d/dx as second map, does not split (Kohlhaase, Corollary 4.3, recalled in Colmez–Nizioł Remark A.6): the Banach hypothesis is essential.
For a finite-dimensional U the statement also follows from Hahn–Banach (Schneider Corollary 9.5).

nodes.title: Compactoid sets and compact maps
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete and V, W Hausdorff locally convex. A subset B ⊆ V is compactoid if for every open lattice L there are v_1, …, v_m ∈ V with B ⊆ L + O_K v_1 + … + O_K v_m. An O_K-submodule A is c-compact if for every decreasingly filtered family of open lattices L_i the map A → lim← A/(L_i ∩ A) is surjective; for a bounded O_K-submodule, c-compact is equivalent to compactoid and complete. Compactoid submodules are bounded, and closures, submodules, finite sums and continuous linear images of compactoid submodules are compactoid. A continuous linear map f : V → W is compact if some open lattice L ⊆ V has f(L) contained in a bounded c-compact submodule (its closure is bounded and c-compact); if W is quasi-complete this means f(L) is compactoid. Compositions h∘f∘g with f compact are compact, and a compact map into a closed subspace stays compact there. Between Banach spaces f is compact iff its transpose f′ is compact iff f″ maps (V′_b)′ into W. When K is locally compact (finite over ℚ_p), a subset of a Banach space is compactoid iff it is totally bounded, so a continuous linear map between K-Banach spaces is compact in this sense iff it is a Mathlib IsCompactOperator.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete (Schneider, Chapter III, works under this hypothesis); for the comparison with IsCompactOperator, K locally compact.
proofSteps: Definitions and permanence: Schneider §12 (c-compact submodules, Lemma 12.1; compactoids, Lemma 12.4; Proposition 12.7 for the equivalence c-compact and bounded ⇔ compactoid and complete).
Compact maps: definition and Remark 16.3, Remark 16.7 (ideal property), Lemma 16.4 (duality for Banach spaces), Schneider §16.

Locally compact K: if B ⊆ L + O_K v_1 + … + O_K v_m with L an ε-ball, the compact set O_K v_1 + … + O_K v_m is covered by finitely many ε-balls, so B is totally bounded; conversely a finite ε-net lies in the O_K-span of finitely many vectors. A relatively compact image of a ball is then the Mathlib condition that the preimage of a compact set is a zero neighbourhood. This comparison is a direct argument, not a cited statement.
acceptance: The four unit tests below.

nodes.title: Spaces of compact type
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete. A locally convex K-vector space V is of compact type if it is isomorphic to the locally convex inductive limit of a sequence V_1 → V_2 → … of Hausdorff locally convex spaces with injective compact transition maps; one may take the V_n to be Banach spaces. Such a V is Hausdorff, complete, bornological and reflexive; it is regular: every bounded subset of V is the image of a bounded subset of some V_m; its strong dual V′_b is a Fréchet space and the natural map V′_b → lim← (V_n)′_b is a topological isomorphism. Closed subspaces U and the quotients V/U of a space of compact type are of compact type, and the dual sequence 0 → (V/U)′_b → V′_b → U′_b → 0 is algebraically exact with strict maps. Countable locally convex direct sums and finite products of spaces of compact type are of compact type. Spaces of compact type are nuclear, so their bounded subsets are compactoid. An infinite-dimensional Banach space is never of compact type (it is not reflexive).
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: Hausdorff and regular: Schneider Lemma 16.9, by building open lattices inductively with Remark 16.8 so as to avoid a given vector, respectively a sequence escaping every stage.
Reflexive, bornological, complete, and the dual as a projective limit: Schneider Proposition 16.10 and Schneider–Teitelbaum Theorem 1.1.
Subspaces, quotients and the strict dual sequence: Schneider–Teitelbaum Proposition 1.2(i); direct sums: Proposition 1.2(ii).
Nuclearity: Schneider Proposition 19.9 (compact inductive limits are nuclear), and bounded = compactoid by Proposition 19.2.
Banach spaces: an infinite-dimensional Banach space over a spherically complete field is not reflexive (Schneider Proposition 11.1).
acceptance: The five unit tests below.

nodes.title: Nuclear spaces
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete. For an open lattice L of a locally convex V let V̂_L be the Hausdorff completion of V for the gauge p_L (a K-Banach space); for open lattices M ⊆ L there is a canonical map V̂_M → V̂_L. V is nuclear if for every open lattice L there is an open lattice M ⊆ L with V̂_M → V̂_L compact; equivalently every continuous linear map from V to a K-Banach space is compact; equivalently (for the compactoid formulation) for every open lattice L there is an open lattice M ⊆ L such that M is compactoid modulo L: for every n there are finitely many v_i with M ⊆ π^n L + Σ O_K v_i. Finite-dimensional spaces and weak topologies are nuclear; a nuclear Banach space is finite-dimensional. In a nuclear space bounded and compactoid subsets coincide; quasi-complete nuclear spaces are semi-reflexive and nuclear Fréchet spaces are reflexive. Subspaces and quotients by closed subspaces of nuclear spaces are nuclear; arbitrary products and countable locally convex direct sums of nuclear spaces are nuclear; compact projective limits and compact inductive limits are nuclear; projective tensor products of nuclear spaces are nuclear. A Fréchet space is nuclear iff it is the projective limit of a sequence of Banach spaces with compact transition maps.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: Definition and the Banach case: Schneider §19, printed pp. 127–128.
Equivalent criterion: Proposition 19.5 (every map to a Banach space is compact).
Bounded = compactoid and reflexivity: Proposition 19.2 and Corollary 19.3.

Permanence: Proposition 19.4 (subspaces, quotients), Proposition 19.7 (products, countable sums), Proposition 19.9 (compact limits), Proposition 19.11 (projective tensor products, using Lemma 18.12 and Lemma 19.10).

Fréchet characterisation: a compact projective limit of Banach spaces is a reflexive Fréchet space (Corollary 16.6) and nuclear (Proposition 19.9); conversely for nuclear Fréchet V the spaces V̂_{L_n} for a decreasing basis of lattices with compact transitions present V.
The compactoid formulation is Colmez–Gilles–Nizioł Definition 2.4; for complete Banach targets compactness of V̂_M → V̂_L means the image of M is compactoid in V̂_L (Schneider Proposition 12.7).
acceptance: The four unit tests below.

nodes.title: Duality between spaces of compact type and nuclear Fréchet spaces
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete. (i) A K-Fréchet space is the strong dual of a space of compact type iff it is nuclear. (ii) V ↦ V′_b is an anti-equivalence from the category of spaces of compact type to the category of nuclear Fréchet spaces, with quasi-inverse F ↦ F′_b; for spaces of compact type V and W the transpose L_b(V, W) → L_b(W′_b, V′_b) is a topological isomorphism. (iii) Both classes are reflexive; on them the strong dual coincides with the stereotype dual (uniform convergence on compactoid sets). (iv) For a projective system of Banach spaces (V_n) with compact transitions and dense projections, P : lim→ (V_n)′_b → (lim← V_n)′_b is a topological isomorphism and lim← V_n is a reflexive Fréchet space; dually, for a compact inductive system the map (lim→ V_n)′_b → lim← (V_n)′_b is a topological isomorphism.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: (i) Schneider–Teitelbaum Theorem 1.3, through Komatsu's and Gruson–van der Put's results; the compact-limit description of nuclear Fréchet spaces is in nuclear-spaces.
(ii) Applying the strong dual twice gives the identity by reflexivity, and the transpose is continuous with continuous inverse (Corollary 1.4).

nodes.title: Completed tensor products of spaces of compact type
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete and V = lim→ V_n, W = lim→ W_n spaces of compact type presented by Banach spaces with injective compact transitions. Then (i) V ⊗_ι W = V ⊗_π W (inductive-tensor-product (c)) and the natural map lim→ (V_n ⊗̂ W_n) → V ⊗̂ W is a topological isomorphism; the transitions V_n ⊗̂ W_n → V_{n+1} ⊗̂ W_{n+1} are injective and compact, so V ⊗̂ W is of compact type; (ii) its strong dual is V′_b ⊗̂ W′_b, a nuclear Fréchet space. For nuclear Fréchet spaces F and G, F ⊗̂ G is nuclear Fréchet. These statements make no claim about tensor products of general LF-spaces.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: Lemma 1.1.30 of Emerton (tensor products commute with inductive limits) identifies the algebraic stage limit with V ⊗ W topologically; banach-completed-tensor-injective supplies injectivity even though the stage maps need not be embeddings; Schneider Lemma 18.12 supplies compactness, so the completed stages form an injective compact system (tensor products of compact maps are compact, Schneider Lemma 18.12), so their limit is of compact type and complete, and it is the completion of V ⊗ W (Emerton Proposition 1.1.32(i)).

Duality: Emerton Proposition 1.1.32(ii); nuclearity of the Fréchet tensor product: Emerton Proposition 1.1.28 and Schneider Proposition 19.11. Apply Schneider Proposition 20.13 to the reflexive nuclear Fréchet duals and use compact-type-nuclear-duality to transpose the resulting isomorphism; this is the argument in Emerton 1.1.32(ii).
The diagonal choice of stages (V_n ⊗ W_n) is cofinal in the double system (V_m ⊗ W_n).
acceptance: K^(ℕ) ⊗̂ K^(ℕ) = K^(ℕ×ℕ) (compact type), dual to K^ℕ ⊗̂ K^ℕ = K^{ℕ×ℕ}.

nodes.title: Nuclearity of strict extensions
nodes.statement: Let 0 → A → B → C → 0 be a strict short exact sequence of nonarchimedean locally convex K-spaces (A carries the topology induced from B and B → C is open and surjective). If A and C are nuclear, then B is nuclear. In particular a strict extension of nuclear Fréchet spaces is a nuclear Fréchet space (the Fréchet property being Colmez–Nizioł Proposition A.3). This is the nonarchimedean counterpart of Dierolf–Roelcke Proposition 3.8, which is proved for real and complex locally convex spaces by absolutely summable sequences; Colmez–Nizioł use it for nonarchimedean Fréchet spaces without comment (source issue E101). The proof below uses only lattices.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.

Nuclearity in the lattice form of nuclear-spaces (for every open lattice L there is an open lattice M ⊆ L with M compactoid modulo π^n L for all n); K spherically complete when this is compared with Schneider's definition.
proofSteps: Let L be an open lattice of B. Since A is nuclear there is an open lattice M_A of A, M_A ⊆ L ∩ A, such that for every n there is a finite set F_n ⊆ A with M_A ⊆ π^n(L ∩ A) + O_K F_n. Because A carries the induced topology, there is an open lattice L′ ⊆ L of B with L′ ∩ A ⊆ M_A.

Since B → C is open, π_C(L′) is an open lattice of C; since C is nuclear there is an open lattice M_C ⊆ π_C(L′) such that for every n there is a finite set G_n ⊆ B with M_C ⊆ π^n π_C(L′) + O_K π_C(G_n).

Put M = L′ ∩ π_C^{-1}(M_C), an open lattice of B contained in L. Fix n and b ∈ M. Then π_C(b) = π^n π_C(l′) + Σ_g λ_g π_C(g) with l′ ∈ L′ and λ_g ∈ O_K, so a := b − π^n l′ − Σ_g λ_g g lies in A. Choose k_n ≥ 0 with G_n ⊆ π^{-k_n} L′ (a finite set is absorbed by a lattice); then a ∈ π^{-k_n} L′ ∩ A ⊆ π^{-k_n} M_A ⊆ π^n (L ∩ A) + O_K π^{-k_n} F_{n+k_n}.
Hence b ∈ π^n L + O_K G_n + O_K π^{-k_n} F_{n+k_n}, a finite O_K-span modulo π^n L, for every n: M is compactoid modulo L, and B is nuclear.
Fréchet case: B is Fréchet by Colmez–Nizioł Proposition A.3 (LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/frechet-three-space), and nuclear by the above.
acceptance: A = K, C = c₀(ℕ, K): B = K ⊕ c₀ is not nuclear, consistent with C not being nuclear.
The non-split strict sequence 0 → tR⁺ → R⁺ → R⁺/t → 0 of Colmez–Nizioł Remark A.6 has nuclear Fréchet terms throughout, as the theorem requires.
For A finite-dimensional the statement is also Colmez–Gilles–Nizioł Lemma 2.5(2) (finite-rank-strict-splitting).

nodes.title: Strict extensions by finite-dimensional spaces split
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete. (1) A strict short exact sequence 0 → V → W → W′ → 0 of locally convex K-spaces with V finite-dimensional and W′ Hausdorff splits topologically: W ≅ V ⊕ W′. Equivalently, every extension of a Hausdorff space by K in LH(NACvx K) is trivial (the separated Ext¹-vanishing used by Colmez–Nizioł for Proposition A.4). (2) Consequently, if W′ is nuclear Fréchet (respectively of compact type), so is W. (3) In a map of strict exact sequences of complete Hausdorff spaces from 0 → V → W → W′ → 0 to 0 → V_1 → W_1 → W′_1 → 0 with V, V_1 finite-dimensional and the second sequence split, compactness of the map on the quotients implies compactness of the map on the middle terms. (4) For any strict short exact sequence 0 → W_1 → W → W_2 → 0 the restriction W′ → W_1′ of continuous linear forms is surjective (Hahn–Banach), so the algebraic dual sequence 0 → W_2′ → W′ → W_1′ → 0 is exact.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: (1) In dimension one choose e∈V and a continuous λ with λ(e)≠0 by Hahn–Banach. The continuous projector P(w)=λ(w)λ(e)^{−1}e has P|V=id. The mutually inverse continuous maps w↦(P(w),w−P(w)) and (v,u)↦v+u identify W with V⊕ker λ. Strictness of the quotient identifies ker λ homeomorphically with W′. Iterate for finite-dimensional V; dimension zero is immediate. This avoids an unsupported openness computation with lattices.
(2) W ≅ V ⊕ W′ with V finite-dimensional, and finite products preserve nuclear Fréchet spaces and spaces of compact type.
(3) Colmez–Gilles–Nizioł Lemma 2.7: correct f_W by a section of the split bottom sequence and use compactoid images.
(4) Schneider Corollary 9.4 extends continuous forms from the subspace W_1; equivalently push the extension out along the form and split it by (1).
acceptance: 0 → K → K ⊕ c₀ → c₀ → 0 splits, as (1) requires.
For the strict sequence 0 → c_c(ℕ, K) → c₀(ℕ, K) → c₀/c_c → 0 the quotient is not Hausdorff and the subspace not finite-dimensional; (1) does not apply.

nodes.title: Duality step for strict extensions of spaces of compact type
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete and 0 → W_1 → W → W_2 → 0 a strict short exact sequence with W_1 and W_2 of compact type. (a) W is Hausdorff, W_1 is closed in W, the dual sequence 0 → (W_2)′ → W′ → (W_1)′ → 0 is algebraically exact, the transposes (W_2)′_b → W′_b and W′_b → (W_1)′_b are continuous, and the image of (W_2)′ is the annihilator of W_1, closed in W′_b. (b) Suppose (H1) the strong dual sequence 0 → (W_2)′_b → W′_b → (W_1)′_b → 0 is strictly exact. Then W′_b is a nuclear Fréchet space, its strong dual W″ = (W′_b)′_b is of compact type, and the double dual sequence 0 → W_1 → W″ → W_2 → 0 (through the duality isomorphisms W_i ≅ (W_i′_b)′_b) is strictly exact. (c) Suppose moreover (H2) the canonical map W → W″ is continuous (for instance W barrelled). Then W → W″ is a topological isomorphism and W is of compact type. Neither (H1) nor (H2) is established here for a general strict extension; both are recorded as the gap 'Strict duality for extensions of spaces of compact type'. These are sufficient strong-dual inputs for a repair of Colmez–Nizioł Proposition A.4; the source instead uses stereotype duals, whose topology on the unknown middle term is not shown to be the strong topology (source issue E102).
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
K spherically complete.
proofSteps: (a) Hausdorffness and closedness of W_1 are left-heart-classical-extensions; algebraic exactness is finite-rank-strict-splitting (4) together with the universal property of the quotient topology; continuity of transposes is bounded-sets-strong-dual; the annihilator of W_1 is closed in the weak topology, hence in the strong one.

(b) Under (H1), W′_b is a strict extension of the nuclear Fréchet spaces (W_1)′_b and (W_2)′_b, hence Fréchet (LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/frechet-three-space) and nuclear (nuclear-three-space); so W″ is of compact type (compact-type-nuclear-duality).

Double dual: the image U of (W_1′_b)′_b → W″ is the annihilator of (W_2)′_b, a closed subspace of the space of compact type W″; restriction W″ → (W_2′_b)′_b is surjective (Hahn–Banach) with kernel U, and it and the bijection (W_1′_b)′_b → U are open by the open mapping theorem for LF-spaces (Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł §2.1.2), since all four spaces are of compact type (Schneider–Teitelbaum Proposition 1.2(i) for U). With the duality isomorphisms this gives the strict sequence 0 → W_1 → W″ → W_2 → 0.

(c) Under (H2) the canonical map W → W″ is a morphism of strict extensions inducing the identity on W_1 and W_2; by the five lemma in LH(NACvx K) it is an isomorphism there, hence (left-heart-classical-extensions) a topological isomorphism, and W is of compact type.
acceptance: If W = W_1 ⊕ W_2 topologically, (H1) and (H2) hold and W is of compact type by compact-type-spaces (finite direct sums).
If W_1 is finite-dimensional, finite-rank-strict-splitting gives the conclusion without (H1) or (H2).

nodes.title: Power series converging on a closed polydisc
nodes.statement: For ε > 0, r ∈ ℕ and a K-Banach space V, F_ε(K^r; V) is the space of formal power series f = Σ_α X^α v_α (α ∈ ℕ^r, v_α ∈ V) with ε^{|α|}‖v_α‖ → 0 along the cofinite filter, normed by ‖f‖_ε = max_α ε^{|α|}‖v_α‖. It is a K-Banach space whose limits are computed coefficientwise, and for ε = |c| with c ∈ K^× the map (a_α) ↦ Σ a_α c^{−|α|} X^α is an isometry c₀(ℕ^r, K) ≅ F_ε(K^r; K). Evaluation f ↦ f̃(x) = Σ x^α v_α at x in the closed polydisc B_ε(0) ⊆ K^r (max norm) is continuous of norm ≤ 1. A continuous bilinear map V_1 × V_2 → V induces a continuous bilinear Cauchy product F_ε(K^r; V_1) × F_ε(K^r; V_2) → F_ε(K^r; V) compatible with evaluation; F_ε(K^r; K) is a commutative K-algebra with multiplicative norm ‖fg‖_ε = ‖f‖_ε‖g‖_ε. Re-expanding f at another point y ∈ B_ε(0) gives a series in F_ε(K^r; V) with the same norm and the same function on the ball. In characteristic 0 the identity theorem holds: f̃ determines f, so F_ε(K^r; V) is a space of functions on B_ε(0). For V = K this is Mathlib's MvPowerSeries.IsRestricted at the constant radius ε, and ‖f‖_ε is Mathlib's MvPowerSeries.gaussNorm with the absolute value and the constant radius ε. In one variable, re-centred at a, this is the space An(B(a, s), L) of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/disc-analytic-functions for ε = p^{−s}. Ownership: for scalar coefficients the carrier, multiplication, Gauss normed ring, completeness, normed algebra and multiplicativity are existing Mathlib/current Tau Ceti work, not new targets here. The new construction is the Banach-valued coefficient model with evaluation, c₀ comparison and re-expansion. The scalar aliases only express compatibility at the older pins. Mixed-base adapter: for finite L/ℚ_p and a complete coefficient extension K/L, define F_ε(L^r;V) by the same coefficient decay and Gauss norm for a K-Banach V, evaluating only on L-points. Apply the Banach-valued construction over L to the underlying L-Banach space of V, then retain the coefficientwise K-action to obtain a K-Banach stage. Evaluation is injective by the characteristic-zero identity theorem over L. For scalar V=K, the formal-series carrier is still MvPowerSeries (Fin r) K; no new scalar Tate algebra is needed.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
For the identity theorem, K has characteristic 0.
proofSteps: Banach property and coefficientwise limits: Schneider, p-Adic Lie Groups §5, printed pp. 25–26, identifying F_ε with a weighted c₀ space; the norm depends only on the topology of V (Remark after the definition).
Evaluation: Remark 5.1 bounds |f̃(x)| by ‖f‖_ε for x ∈ B_ε(0).

Use existing scalar multiplication closure MvPowerSeries.isRestricted.mul at the Mathlib pin, and the scalar normed-ring, completeness, normed-algebra and multiplicativity instances in current Tau Ceti TateAlgebra.Basic. For Banach-valued Cauchy products use the bounded bilinear coefficient pairing of Schneider Proposition 5.2; retain the evaluation comparison as the new API.
Change of centre: Corollary 5.5; identity theorem: Corollary 5.8.
Mathlib: with c = (fun _ ↦ ε), t.prod (c · ^ ·) = ε^{|t|}, so MvPowerSeries.IsRestricted c f is the decay condition and gaussNorm is ‖f‖_ε.

Mixed-base stages: regard a K-Banach V as an L-Banach space, apply the Banach-valued power-series and identity theorem over L, and observe that the coefficient norm and all evaluation/substitution maps respect the K-action. This is the coefficient extension in ST99 §2 and Emerton (0.1–0.3), not an assumption that ℤ_p is a positive-dimensional K-manifold when K≠ℚ_p.

nodes.title: Substitution of power series on polydiscs
nodes.statement: Let g = (g_1, …, g_n) ∈ F_δ(K^r; K^n) with ‖g‖_δ = max_i ‖g_i‖_δ ≤ ε. Then for every K-Banach space V the substitution f(Y) = Σ_β Y^β v_β ↦ f∘g(X) = Σ_β g(X)^β v_β is a well-defined continuous linear map F_ε(K^n; V) → F_δ(K^r; V) of operator norm ≤ 1, and (f∘g)~(x) = f̃(g̃(x)) for x ∈ B_δ(0). The constant term of g need not vanish: the hypothesis says that g maps B_δ(0) into B_ε(0) with norm control. Special cases: restriction from radius ε to a radius δ ≤ ε (g = X), translation to a centre y ∈ B_ε(0), and the affine changes of variable x ↦ a + cx of residue-ball charts; the norm bound gives the refinement inclusions of chart indices and the stagewise pullback of locally analytic maps. Mathlib's MvPowerSeries.subst requires substituted series with nilpotent constant coefficients and does not cover this case.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Proposition 5.3 gives ‖g^β‖_δ = Π ‖g_i‖_δ^{β_i} ≤ ε^{|β|}, so Σ_β g^β v_β converges in F_δ(K^r; V) with ‖f∘g‖_δ ≤ max_β ε^{|β|}‖v_β‖ = ‖f‖_ε (Schneider, p-Adic Lie Groups, Proposition 5.4).
Evaluation is continuous (Remark 5.1) and multiplicative, so (f∘g)~ = f̃∘g̃ on B_δ(0).

nodes.title: Locally analytic manifolds, charts and atlases
nodes.statement: Let M be a Hausdorff topological space. An n-dimensional chart for M is a triple (U, φ, K^n) with U ⊆ M open and φ : U → K^n a homeomorphism onto an open subset. Two charts are compatible if both transition maps φ_2∘φ_1^{-1} and φ_1∘φ_2^{-1} are locally analytic on their domains (locally given by convergent power series); compatible charts with intersecting domains have the same dimension. An atlas is a family of pairwise compatible charts covering M; atlases are equivalent if their union is an atlas; each equivalence class has a unique maximal atlas, and a (locally K-analytic) manifold is M with a maximal atlas. A map between manifolds is locally analytic if it is so in charts; open subsets and finite products of manifolds are manifolds. M is paracompact iff it is strictly paracompact (every open covering is refined by a covering by pairwise disjoint open subsets), and then it is a disjoint union of open subsets each of which is the domain of a chart whose image is a closed ball; in particular every compact manifold is, for every open covering, a finite disjoint union of chart domains with ball images refining it. Over a finite extension F of ℚ_p the ring O_F is a manifold over F of dimension 1 and, by restriction of scalars through a ℤ_p-basis, a manifold over ℚ_p of dimension [F : ℚ_p] (LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/field-analytic-functions compares the two). A K-analytic manifold structure of dimension n on M amounts to a Mathlib ChartedSpace (Fin n → K) M with HasGroupoid for contDiffGroupoid ω, where ω-smoothness is analyticity because K^n is complete; Mathlib's IsManifold 𝓘(K, Fin n → K) ω M is then the same notion. Ownership: on each component of fixed dimension reuse OpenPartialHomeomorph, ChartedSpace, HasGroupoid, IsManifold at analytic regularity ω, and ContMDiff ω. The targets are the power-series compatibility theorem, ball refinements and change-of-scalar adapters. A varying-dimensional manifold is a disjoint union of these components, rather than a second manifold carrier. For the following function-space targets instantiate this manifold structure over the base field L, retaining K as the separate coefficient extension.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.
proofSteps: Compatibility and dimension: Schneider, p-Adic Lie Groups, Lemma 7.1 (by the chain rule the derivatives of the two transition maps are inverse linear maps, so the dimensions agree); equivalence of atlases and maximal atlases: Remark 7.2 and Lemma 7.3; refinements of atlases: Remark 7.4.

Manifolds and maps: §8, Remark 8.1 (restriction of charts), Lemmas 8.3–8.4 (locally analytic maps and composition); open submanifolds and products are manifolds, and they are paracompact when M is (Corollary 8.8).

Paracompactness: Remark 8.6 (ultrametric spaces are strictly paracompact, compact spaces paracompact) and Proposition 8.7 (paracompact ⇔ strictly paracompact ⇔ the topology is given by a metric with the strict triangle inequality); a strictly paracompact manifold is a disjoint union of chart domains with ball images, by refining a chart covering by disjoint balls (Lemma 1.4) and restricting charts (Remark 8.1); compact manifolds are strictly paracompact (Schneider–Teitelbaum §2, printed p. 5).

Mathlib: a chart in this sense is an OpenPartialHomeomorph; the analytic groupoid condition is contDiffGroupoid ω (Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.IsManifold.Basic), and for maps between open subsets of complete spaces ContDiffOn ω is analyticity (the ω-case of ContDiffWithinAt).

nodes.title: Indices and their Banach stages
nodes.statement: Let M be a paracompact L-analytic manifold and E a K-Banach space. For a chart c = (U, φ, L^m) and ε > 0 with φ(U) = B_ε(a) a closed ball, F_{(c,ε)}(E) is the space of functions f : U → E such that f∘φ^{-1}(x) = F(x − a) for some F ∈ F_ε(L^m; E), with ‖f‖ = ‖F‖_ε; it is a Banach space, independent of the centre a. An index I = {(c_i, ε_i)}_{i∈I} is a family of such charts whose domains U_i are pairwise disjoint and cover M; its stage is F_I(E) = Π_i F_{(c_i,ε_i)}(E) ⊆ C^an(M, E) with the product topology (a Banach space when I is finite, which is automatic for compact M). An index I is finer than J if every U_i lies in some V_j with ψ_j∘φ_i^{-1}(x) = F_{ij}(x − a_i) and ‖F_{ij} − F_{ij}(0)‖_{ε_i} ≤ δ_j; then F_J(E) ⊆ F_I(E) and the inclusion is continuous, of norm ≤ 1 factorwise; any two indices have a common finer index; and the topology of F_J(E) is in general strictly finer than the one induced from F_I(E). For M = ℤ_p and the index I_h of residue balls a + p^hℤ_p with the identity charts and radius p^{−h}, F_{I_h}(K) = LA_h(ℤ_p, K) isometrically; the coefficient model of a finite index with normalised coordinates is c₀(S × ℕ^d, K) as in LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/multivariable-fixed-radius.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.

In the geometric strand L is a finite extension of ℚ_p, K is a complete nonarchimedean extension of L with compatible absolute value, and M is an L-analytic manifold. Coefficient Banach spaces are over K. Compact-type and nuclear-dual assertions additionally require K spherically complete. The special case L=K recovers the self-base notation of p-Adic Lie Groups.
M is paracompact (strictly paracompact), E a K-Banach space. Finite chart indices are automatic for compact M; ST99 also allows BH-subspaces of a general coefficient space.
proofSteps: Banach stages and independence of the centre: Schneider, p-Adic Lie Groups §10, using the identity theorem and Corollary 5.5.

Refinement: Lemma 10.1 (F_J ⊆ F_I, by substituting the transition expansions with Proposition 5.4), Lemma 10.2 (common refinement: cover the chart overlaps by small disjoint balls on which the transition maps expand, then shrink radii so that the transition norms are ≤ δ_j), Lemma 10.3 (continuity of the inclusion, of norm ≤ 1 by Proposition 5.4), and the remark after it (the topologies differ).
Schneider–Teitelbaum describe the same stages through V-indices {(D_i, φ_i, V_i)} with F_{φ_i}(V_i) ≅ O(φ_i(D_i)) ⊗̂ V_i (§2, printed pp. 5–6).
Comparison with LA_h: on a + p^hℤ_p the identity chart has image B_{p^{−h}}(a), and F_{p^{−h}}(K; K) at centre a is the space An(B(a, h), K) of the predecessor, with the same Gauss norm.

nodes.title: Restriction to smaller polydiscs is compact
nodes.statement: Let 0 < δ < ε. The restriction map F_ε(L^m; K) → F_δ(L^m; K) (same centre) satisfies ‖f − T_N f‖_δ ≤ (δ/ε)^N ‖f‖_ε, where T_N f is the truncation of f to total degree < N; hence it is a compact map, the image of the unit ball being compactoid. Consequently, if a finite index I of a compact L-analytic manifold is a relatively compact refinement of a finite index J (on each source chart the target-coordinate transition, re-centred at its constant term, has Gauss norm ≤ η < δ_j, where δ_j is the target chart radius), the inclusion F_J(K) → F_I(K) is injective and compact; this is the polydisc specialization of the affinoid result of Emerton Proposition 2.1.16. In particular LA_h(ℤ_p, K) → LA_{h+1}(ℤ_p, K) is injective and compact.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.

In the geometric strand L is a finite extension of ℚ_p, K is a complete nonarchimedean extension of L with compatible absolute value, and M is an L-analytic manifold. Coefficient Banach spaces are over K. Compact-type and nuclear-dual assertions additionally require K spherically complete. The special case L=K recovers the self-base notation of p-Adic Lie Groups.

The scalar restriction map has coefficient field K and L-coordinate balls; the general affinoid claim of Emerton 2.1.16 is cited only by this ball specialization, and general affinoid algebras retain their rigid-geometry owner.
proofSteps: Truncation estimate: a coefficient v_α with |α| ≥ N contributes δ^{|α|}‖v_α‖ ≤ (δ/ε)^{|α|} ε^{|α|}‖v_α‖ ≤ (δ/ε)^N ‖f‖_ε.

The image of the unit ball therefore lies, modulo the ball of radius (δ/ε)^N, in the bounded set of polynomials of degree < N with coefficients bounded by ε^{−|α|}, which is contained in a finitely generated O_K-module: the image is compactoid (compactoid-compact-maps).

For a chart change first restrict the target series from radius δ_j to the intermediate target-coordinate radius η < δ_j, after re-centring. Then substitute the transition expansion, whose nonconstant Gauss norm is ≤ η, using multivariate-substitution-bound. Compactness of the first map and boundedness of the second give compactness of their composite. Radii from different coordinate charts cannot be compared directly. Take finite products for finite indices.
Injectivity: the identity theorem on the smaller ball (restricted-power-series-ball). The affinoid formulation is Emerton Proposition 2.1.16.
acceptance: For m = 1, ε = 1 and δ = 1/p the unit vectors X^n have images of norm p^{−n} → 0: the restriction is a compact diagonal operator.
For δ = ε the restriction is the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space, which is not compact: strict inequality of radii is needed.
This gives the compactness input of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/radius-restriction-compact with the explicit constant 1 in normalised coordinates.

nodes.title: Locally analytic functions on a manifold
nodes.statement: Let M be a paracompact L-analytic manifold and E a K-Banach space. The space of locally analytic functions C^an(M, E) = ⋃_I F_I(E), the union over all indices of M, carries the locally convex inductive limit topology of the stages F_I(E) along the refinement order. It is Hausdorff; evaluation at each point is continuous; for every partition M = ⊔_j M_j into open subsets, C^an(M, E) = Π_j C^an(M_j, E) topologically; and the map C^an(M, E) → C(M, E) is a continuous injection with dense image (locally constant functions are locally analytic). For a Hausdorff locally convex V, C^an(M, V) is the inductive limit over indices and BH-subspaces of V. The space depends only on the manifold, i.e. on the maximal atlas: any atlas gives cofinal indices, so two atlases defining the same manifold give the same locally convex space. If M is compact: every index can be refined to a finite one, every finite family of functions lies in a common stage, and there exists a cofinal sequence of finite indices I_1 ≤ I_2 ≤ …, each a relatively compact refinement of the previous, constructed with chart mesh tending to zero and the transition-norm refinement bounds, so C^an(M, K) = lim→ F_{I_n}(K) is of compact type; its strong dual D(M, K) = C^an(M, K)′_b is a nuclear Fréchet space equal to lim← F_{I_n}(K)′_b. For M = ℤ_p this is LA(ℤ_p, K) = lim→ LA_h(ℤ_p, K) of the predecessor, with the same topology.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.

In the geometric strand L is a finite extension of ℚ_p, K is a complete nonarchimedean extension of L with compatible absolute value, and M is an L-analytic manifold. Coefficient Banach spaces are over K. Compact-type and nuclear-dual assertions additionally require K spherically complete. The special case L=K recovers the self-base notation of p-Adic Lie Groups.
M is paracompact; C(M,E) carries the compact-open topology. For the countable cofinal compact-type/dual assertions M is compact and K spherically complete.
proofSteps: Inductive limit: Schneider, p-Adic Lie Groups §12, printed p. 84 (using Lemmas 10.1–10.3 to form the inductive system); Hausdorffness and evaluation: Proposition 12.1 and Corollary 12.2; disjoint decompositions: Proposition 12.5 (also Schneider–Teitelbaum §2 after Féaux de Lacroix).
Dense injection into C(M, E): Emerton Proposition 2.1.26.

Independence of the atlas: the indices are formed from charts of the maximal atlas, and Lemma 10.2 shows that the indices built from any atlas are cofinal; chart-wise, the identity of M is locally analytic and its stagewise substitutions have norm ≤ 1 (multivariate-substitution-bound), so it induces continuous maps between the two inductive limits in both directions.

For compact M and L finite over ℚ_p, choose a finite initial ball partition and recursively refine it by residue balls of mesh tending to zero, shrinking further to satisfy all transition-norm bounds. Local analytic expansions and compactness show that every index is eventually refined: this proves cofinality, rather than assuming every sequence of strictly shrinking radii is cofinal. Scalar restriction maps are injective compact by relatively-compact-restriction, giving compact type and the dual statements. A finite family lies in one common refined stage.

M = ℤ_p: the residue-ball indices I_h are cofinal among indices of ℤ_p (every ball chart of ℤ_p is refined by residue balls, and arbitrary analytic chart transitions satisfy the Gauss-norm bound after sufficiently fine shrinking; affine transitions occur only among the standard residue charts), so the two inductive limits agree (chart-index-banach-stages).

nodes.title: Pullback and multiplication of locally analytic functions
nodes.statement: Let g : M → N be a locally analytic map of paracompact L-analytic manifolds and E a K-Banach space. (i) For every index J of N there is an index I of M such that f ↦ f∘g maps F_J(E) into F_I(E) with norm ≤ 1 on each factor; hence g^* : C^an(N, E) → C^an(M, E) is a continuous linear map, with (g∘h)^* = h^*∘g^* and id^* = id. (ii) For a fixed a ∈ C^an(M, K), multiplication by a is a continuous endomorphism of C^an(M, E), mapping F_I(E) into F_{I′}(E) for a common refinement I′ of I and a stage containing a, with bound the stage norm of a. These are maps of actual functions, in contrast with transposes of arbitrary given continuous maps; both preserve bounded sets, so their transposes are continuous on strong duals.

nodes.title: Locally analytic functions on products
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete and X, Y compact L-analytic manifolds. The external product (f, g) ↦ ((x, y) ↦ f(x)g(y)) induces a topological isomorphism C^an(X, K) ⊗̂ C^an(Y, K) ≅ C^an(X × Y, K), where ⊗̂ is the completed projective tensor product, equal to the inductive one because both factors are of compact type. At the level of stages: for finite indices I of X and J of Y chosen cofinally with radii in |L^×| and normalized to radius one on all charts, the product charts form a finite index I × J of X × Y and F_I(K) ⊗̂ F_J(K) ≅ F_{I×J}(K) isometrically, F_ε(L^m; K) ⊗̂ F_ε(L^n; K) ≅ F_ε(L^{m+n}; K) being the c₀(ℕ^m) ⊗̂ c₀(ℕ^n) ≅ c₀(ℕ^{m+n}) identification. Product indices are cofinal among indices of X × Y.

Coefficient Banach spaces are over K. Compact-type and nuclear-dual assertions additionally require K spherically complete. The special case L=K recovers the self-base notation of p-Adic Lie Groups.
X and Y are compact; the normalized cofinal chart radii are in |L^×|, so they can be scaled using L×.
proofSteps: Rescale chosen value-group-radius charts to unit radius. Then both scalar stages are c₀ of their multi-index sets, and c0-completed-tensor gives the stage isometry by concatenating multi-indices. Scalar coefficient flattening in unit-radius Tate algebras already exists in current Tau Ceti as TauCeti.Huber.restrictedOptionEquiv and isometry_restrictedOptionEquiv; this target supplies the topological tensor comparison and its stage/limit compatibility, not that scalar flattening again.

For compact X and Y over finite L/ℚ_p, start with product neighbourhoods subordinate to a finite target index on X×Y and shrink them so that every transition expansion satisfies the refinement norm bound. A finite subcover exists. Choose sufficiently fine finite residue-ball partitions separately on X and Y; compactness gives a common mesh such that their entire rectangular grid refines the finite subcover with those bounds. After common rescaling to value-group radii this is a product index refining the target. Finitely many disjoint rectangles alone need not form a product grid.

Limits: choose cofinal relatively compact sequences I_n, J_n; then the I_n × J_n are cofinal in X × Y, and lim→ (F_{I_n}(K) ⊗̂ F_{J_n}(K)) = C^an(X, K) ⊗̂ C^an(Y, K) by compact-type-tensor-products, while the left side is C^an(X × Y, K) by locally-analytic-function-space.

This is a derivation from the cited stage and limit results; it is not stated in this form in the sources read. Emerton Proposition 2.1.28 gives the related C^la(X, V) ≅ C^la(X, K) ⊗̂ V for V of compact type.

nodes.title: Distributions on a compact manifold
nodes.statement: Let K be spherically complete and X a compact L-analytic manifold. C^an(X, K) is of compact type and reflexive; D(X, K) = C^an(X, K)′_b is a nuclear Fréchet space, the natural map D(X, K) → lim← F_{I_n}(K)′_b over a cofinal sequence of relatively compact finite indices is a topological isomorphism, and C^an(X, K) = D(X, K)′_b. The Dirac distributions δ_x (x ∈ X) are elements of D(X, K) and span a dense subspace. For compact X and Y, D(X × Y, K) ≅ D(X, K) ⊗̂ D(Y, K) with δ_{(x,y)} ↦ δ_x ⊗ δ_y. Transposes of the continuous maps g^* and of multiplications by locally analytic functions are continuous on strong duals; g_* = (g^*)′ sends δ_x to δ_{g(x)}. For X = ℤ_p and K finite over ℚ_p, D(ℤ_p, K) is the space of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/locally-analytic-distributions, with the projective-limit topology equal to the strong dual topology.
hypotheses: K is a field complete for a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value |·|, with ring of integers O_K = {a : |a| ≤ 1} and a fixed π ∈ K with 0 < |π| < 1; a lattice in a K-vector space V is an O_K-submodule L with K·L = V.

In the geometric strand L is a finite extension of ℚ_p, K is a complete nonarchimedean extension of L with compatible absolute value, and M is an L-analytic manifold. X is compact, and K is spherically complete; for the product comparison Y is compact as well.
proofSteps: Compact type, reflexivity and the projective-limit description: locally-analytic-function-space and compact-type-nuclear-duality (Schneider–Teitelbaum Lemma 2.1, Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.4).

Density of Dirac distributions: a continuous linear form on D(X, K) is evaluation at some f ∈ C^an(X, K) by reflexivity, and it vanishes on all δ_x iff f = 0; apply Hahn–Banach (nonarchimedean-hahn-banach, Corollary 9.3).

Transposes: bounded-sets-strong-dual and locally-analytic-pullback; g_*δ_x = δ_{g(x)} by evaluation.
Comparison with the predecessor: for X = ℤ_p the stages are the LA_h (locally-analytic-function-space), so the projective limit is lim← D_h.
